source.title: Overcoming the Challenges of Batch Normalization in Federated Learning
source.authors: R. Guerraoui; Rafael Pinot; Geovani Rizk; John Stephan; Francois Taiani

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses batch normalization in federated training and evaluates its own federated method against other BatchNorm implementations. It does not compare BatchNorm with no BatchNorm or measure any claim version's specified effect.
record.gate_note: The CIFAR-10 accuracy results compare federated BatchNorm implementations under varying data heterogeneity and attacks. They do not test the listed versions, so rows are recorded under versions ["none"]. Many further results appear only in figures; no precise values are inferred from those plots.
record.test_reason: The study compares federated BatchNorm implementations with centralized BatchNorm. It reports test accuracy and normalization statistics, without testing BatchNorm versus no normalization, learning-rate tolerance, training error, width, depth, or initialization effects specified by V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that FBN matches centralized BatchNorm performance in their tested federated settings and can resist the evaluated adversarial attacks when combined with robust aggregation.
record.recipe_differences: Federated learning with shared running statistics and bias correction, rather than the claim versions' listed centralized training, architecture, initialization, learning-rate, or normalization comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported performance changes with data heterogeneity and with the use of a robust median defense under attacks. Detailed attack results are primarily figure-only.

fits_no_version.finding: With ten clients and extreme label heterogeneity on CIFAR-10, Naive BatchNorm reaches approximately 17% maximum test accuracy, FixBN reaches 75%, and FBN matches the centralized maximum of 80%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shared running statistics with variance correction can preserve centralized BatchNorm test performance under heterogeneous federated data better than naive federated BatchNorm.

record.problems: The paper reports test accuracy rather than training classification error. Key curves and comparisons are figures, and no uncertainty estimates are stated. The numeric prose results cover selected heterogeneity settings; many attack comparisons are figure-only.
record.rows_left_out: No separately extractable figure-only result rows are included, including the attack comparisons in Figures 4–13 and normalization-distance comparisons in Figure 2c; precise values are not stated in the prose.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error, including random or corrupted labels and model-size or regularization dependencies.
Spurious local minima and the effects of extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Depth degradation, identity shortcuts, deep plain tanh initialization, and Fixup training without normalization.
Initialization effects on training speed, signal and gradient propagation, and trainable depth.
Recovery above the initial stability limit, curvature dynamics, edge-of-stability training, and divergence thresholds.
Accuracy gains per training step and learning-rate tolerance relative to the same network without BatchNorm; normalization-free Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted rows concern method-performance comparisons outside V1–V6. Poor federated BatchNorm accuracy does not challenge V6 without the specified comparison against a network without normalization. The supplied text contains no additional result testing a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, including under corrupted or random labels, is not reported.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student experiment or width sweep.
No comparison of plain and residual networks or depth sweep.
No learning-rate stability or sharpness experiment.
No comparison of BatchNorm with the same network without normalization, and no Fixup experiment.
